Rule: In this pipeline a test is not finished when it passes. It
is finished when it has been observed to fail for the right reason.
That bar is higher than most suites are held to, and it is set there
because the suite is the only unarguable signal in the run: everything
between those two states is a test you are taking on trust.
Skip, only, and the quietest way to a green suite
Two markers in every test framework can silently shrink the suite.
skip excludes a test from the run. It reports as skipped, which at least
appears in the output — though nobody reads a summary line saying 4
passed, 1 skipped any more carefully than one saying 5 passed .
only is the more dangerous of the two. Marking a single test only runs
that test and nothing else , and the suite reports green.

2 Introduction
The picture above is an agent : a program that calls a model in a loop,
runs whatever tool the model asks for, and stops when the model stops
asking. It is what you are going to build.
A workflow is a fixed sequence of jobs that a piece of work passes
through, where each job has one responsibility and a defined output.
An agentic workflow is one in which some of those jobs are carried out
by a language model rather than by a person or by code you wrote in
advance.
What travels along those arrows is one JSON object — which model to
ask, the standing instruction, the tools it may call, and every instruction
and reply so far, because the model keeps nothing between calls. Chapter
1 builds the first few of those fields and Chapter 2 the rest, and Chapter
2 shows the whole object once you have written enough of it to read it.

The parts you are going to build
Agentic workflows do not all need the same parts. A job that classifies
text or drafts a summary satisfies the definition above and never calls a
tool, never loops, and never touches anything outside itself. A pipeline
whose output nobody relies on needs no checking either.
The one built here assumes the harder case: the model acts on something
real, and being confidently wrong is expensive. That case takes two
things. A model has to be able to act, and whatever establishes that the
work is right has to be something other than the run that produced it.
This book divides acting and checking into six parts, and each names
the chapter that builds it.

Chapter 10
Tests That Can Fail
This chapter builds a program that tells a test that works from a test
that cannot fail.
There is a test in almost every codebase that has never failed and never
could. It calls the function, it does something with the result, and it
asserts something that was true before the feature existed and will be
true after it is deleted. It runs green in every build, it appears in the
count, and it is load-bearing in exactly one sense: somebody believes it.
What a test is for here
A regression test is an automated check that a behaviour that works
today still works tomorrow: not a specification, documentation or a
design aid, but a tripwire laid across a behaviour you have decided you
care about.
In a workflow where a model writes the code, regression tests do a job
they do not do in ordinary development.

An agent is a program in a loop with a language model.
The program sends a request with a list of tools the model
may ask for, each described in plain words: what it does,
what arguments it takes, what it returns. The model
replies by naming one and the arguments to give it; it
cannot run anything itself. The program runs what the
model named, puts both the call and its result into the
next request, and sends it again, until the model asks for
nothing more or a limit the program sets ends it.
An agentic workflow is a fixed chain of jobs that a
piece of work passes through from start to finish, where
each job is either an agent or ordinary code. The jobs
run serially, and where several run in parallel, the next
one waits for all of them to finish.
The tools are where anything actually changes: a file
written, a row updated, a service called. The model’s last
reply is not the work.

different from putting the same words in the first user message:

Chapter 1
Talking to a Model
This chapter builds one operation in TypeScript, field by field: you send
some text to a server, and text comes back. An agentic workflow rests
on that operation. Every diagram, review, judge and guard rule in the
twelve chapters after this one is that single operation wrapped in struc-
ture.
What the thing on the other end actually is
A large language model — LLM for short — is a very large mathe-
matical function that takes a sequence of text and produces a probability
distribution over what text comes next. It was fitted to that job by be-
ing shown an enormous quantity of text and repeatedly adjusted until
its guesses about what followed got good. The result is a fixed set of
numbers, called weights, that do not change while you use them.

Giving the Model Hands 41
Watch what happens when you ask for something that needs two steps.
Change the request to:
Read demo/src/slugify.ts and demo/src/cli.ts, then tell me whether the CLI
would print an empty line for the input "///".
The model asks to read one file and you send it. It then asks for the
second file, and tool.ts , whose second loop prints only text blocks,
prints nothing, or a sentence of narration, and exits. The program does
nothing with a second tool_use , because it was written with the number
two hard-coded into it.
The fix is not more code but less structure: stop writing “first request,
second request” and write “keep going until it says it is done.”
That is a loop, and it is the entire subject of the next chapter, which is
also where the thing you have been building finally gets its name.

That
point is the training cutoff , and after it the model knows nothing — not
because it refuses to answer, but because it has no way to distinguish
“after my cutoff” from “does not exist.” Ask about a library released
last month and you will not get “I don’t know.” You will get a fluent,
well-structured answer about a plausible library with plausible functions.
This applies to calling an API that changes. A model fitted before a
parameter was removed will keep using it, and a model fitted before a
new one existed will not reach for it. Both failures look identical from
your side — code that reads perfectly and returns a 400 .
Warning: A model is most confidently wrong about the API of
a fast-moving library, and next most about the library’s own best
practices. From inside the weights, the version it learned is the
library.

64 What It Knows and Forgets
Prompt caching stores the beginning of your request on Anthropic’s
servers so that identical beginnings on later requests do not have to be
processed again. Cached input is billed at a small fraction of the normal
input rate. You opt in by marking a block with cache_control: {
type: "ephemeral" } , which says “cache everything from the start of
the request up to and including this block.”
Three facts govern it:
It is a prefix match, and it is exact. The cache is keyed on the literal
sequence of tokens from the very beginning of the request. Change one
character anywhere in that prefix — one character — and everything
after the change is a cache miss. The order the API assembles things
in is tools , then system , then messages , so a tool schema you rebuild
with a different key order destroys the cache for everything behind it,
without saying so.

The definition, before the code
An agent is a program that lets a model choose its own next action,
repeatedly, until the model decides it is finished.
The definition stops there: no autonomy, no planning, no reasoning, just

wrote.
The cycle that loop runs has a name of its own. The agentic loop is:
send the conversation, read the stop reason, execute any requested tools,
append the results, send again. One pass through that cycle is a turn .

The parts you are going to build
Agentic workflows do not all need the same parts. A job that classifies
text or drafts a summary satisfies the definition above and never calls a
tool, never loops, and never touches anything outside itself. A pipeline
whose output nobody relies on needs no checking either.
The one built here assumes the harder case: the model acts on something
real, and being confidently wrong is expensive. That case takes two
things. A model has to be able to act, and whatever establishes that the
work is right has to be something other than the run that produced it.
This book divides acting and checking into six parts, and each names
the chapter that builds it.

A model call. One HTTP request carrying your instructions and ev-

An agent is a program in a loop with a language model.
The program sends a request with a list of tools the model
may ask for, each described in plain words: what it does,
what arguments it takes, what it returns. The model
replies by naming one and the arguments to give it; it
cannot run anything itself. The program runs what the
model named, puts both the call and its result into the
next request, and sends it again, until the model asks for
nothing more or a limit the program sets ends it.
An agentic workflow is a fixed chain of jobs that a
piece of work passes through from start to finish, where
each job is either an agent or ordinary code. The jobs
run serially, and where several run in parallel, the next
one waits for all of them to finish.
The tools are where anything actually changes: a file
written, a row updated, a service called. The model’s last
reply is not the work.

There is a hard iteration cap
The cap earns a section of its own, immediately below.
Termination, and the failure that costs money
A termination condition is whatever makes the loop stop. runAgent
has three, and you need all three:
1. The model says it is done — end_turn , the normal exit.
2. Something went wrong — max_tokens , refusal , or an unan-
swerable stop reason, the exceptional exit.
3. The iteration cap is reached — maxIterations , the backstop.
Leaving the third one out produces a runaway loop : an agentic loop
that never reaches end_turn and keeps calling the API until something
external stops it. Two mundane causes account for most of them:
• A tool that fails in a way the model reads as retryable. It asks to
read src/index.ts ; there is no such file; it gets ENOENT ; it tries
./src/index.ts ; then src/index.tsx ; then src/ . Forever.

A workflow is a fixed sequence of jobs that a piece of work passes

64 What It Knows and Forgets
Prompt caching stores the beginning of your request on Anthropic’s
servers so that identical beginnings on later requests do not have to be
processed again. Cached input is billed at a small fraction of the normal
input rate. You opt in by marking a block with cache_control: {
type: "ephemeral" } , which says “cache everything from the start of
the request up to and including this block.”
Three facts govern it:
It is a prefix match, and it is exact. The cache is keyed on the literal
sequence of tokens from the very beginning of the request. Change one
character anywhere in that prefix — one character — and everything
after the change is a cache miss. The order the API assembles things
in is tools , then system , then messages , so a tool schema you rebuild
with a different key order destroys the cache for everything behind it,
without saying so.

Stable content goes first. House rules, tool schemas, a large document
you are asking questions about: at the front, marked. Timestamps,
request IDs, the actual question: after the last marked block. If you put
new Date().toISOString() in your system prompt, your cache hit rate
is zero and nothing tells you.
You verify it with usage . cache_read_input_tokens is the only
proof you get. If it is zero across repeated requests that should share a
prefix, something is invalidating it, and the fastest way to find out what
is to shorten the prefix until the number goes up.
A prefix also has to be long enough to store. The floor is a few hundred
tokens and differs from model to model, and a request under it is not
cached and not warned about: written and cached both stay at zero.
The house rules alone are far under it, which is why budget.ts puts

An agent is a program that lets a model choose its own next action,
repeatedly, until the model decides it is finished.

Plausible output is indistinguishable from correct output , not
because models are bad, but because a model produces likely text and
has no separate faculty that checks whether likely and true have come
apart. A better model widens the gap between rate and detectability:
fewer wrong answers, more convincing ones.
Nothing grades its own work. This is not an observation about
language models. It is a structural fact about any evaluator whose only
input is the thing being evaluated, and it is why the reviewers in Chapter
7 were blind to the argument, why the judge in Chapter 9 never met the
builder, and why the judge’s own repairs needed a pass nobody in the
pipeline could perform.
A requirement written after the work describes the work. Chap-
ter 6’s whole argument, and it predates computers.
A rule stated in a prompt is a request , as Chapter 11 argued.

A review conducted without access to the author’s reasoning is a blind
review , and the word is doing precise work: the reviewer is blind to the
argument, not to the code. It sees more of the change than the builder’s
summary ever showed; it simply sees none of the case for it.

A violation is not a finding
A finding , from Chapter 7, is a claim a reviewer makes. A judge weighs

violation would hold the very authority the violation exists to deny it.

severity levels and waivers exist and work; this one has neither,

There is a hard iteration cap

Termination, and the failure that costs money
A termination condition is whatever makes the loop stop. runAgent
has three, and you need all three:
1. The model says it is done — end_turn , the normal exit.
2. Something went wrong — max_tokens , refusal , or an unan-
swerable stop reason, the exceptional exit.
3. The iteration cap is reached — maxIterations , the backstop.

• A tool that fails in a way the model reads as retryable. It asks to

Model performance is not flat across a long context. Material at the very
beginning and the very end of a long input is attended to more reliably
than material in the middle. As the input grows, the fraction of it that
is irrelevant to the current question grows too, and the relevant part
gets harder to pick out. This degradation as context grows is sometimes
called context rot . It does not announce itself: you do not get an error
or a warning. You get answers that are slightly worse, in ways that look
like the model being unimpressive rather than the input being bad.

An agent is a program in a loop with a language model.
The program sends a request with a list of tools the model
may ask for, each described in plain words: what it does,

piece of work passes through from start to finish, where
each job is either an agent or ordinary code. The jobs
run serially, and where several run in parallel, the next

Talking to a Model
This chapter builds one operation in TypeScript, field by field: you send
some text to a server, and text comes back. An agentic workflow rests
on that operation. Every diagram, review, judge and guard rule in the
twelve chapters after this one is that single operation wrapped in struc-
ture.
What the thing on the other end actually is
A large language model — LLM for short — is a very large mathe-
matical function that takes a sequence of text and produces a probability
distribution over what text comes next. It was fitted to that job by be-
ing shown an enormous quantity of text and repeatedly adjusted until
its guesses about what followed got good. The result is a fixed set of
numbers, called weights, that do not change while you use them.

Pro Tip: When a run does something baffling, do not start by re-
reading your system prompt. Start by reading the trace from the
top and locating the first tool result that came back wrong or empty.
Usually the model behaved sensibly given a bad input, and the bad
input came from your own function.

Two hundred and fifty lines of TypeScript that reads your code, edits
it, and stops when it thinks it is done. Everything after this chapter is
about the gap between “thinks it is done” and “is done.”

Chapter 9
Somebody Has to Decide
A judge decides what happens to each finding and records the reason, and
this chapter builds one. Six files hold perhaps fifteen findings between
them. Three of those are wrong, two are the same thing said twice, one
is a preference dressed as a defect, and somewhere in the pile are two
that genuinely must be fixed before this change goes anywhere.
The two ways of not deciding
There are exactly two ways to avoid making the decision.
Fix everything. Take all fifteen findings, hand them back, apply them
all. This fails for a reason that has nothing to do with effort: a third of
the findings are wrong, and applying a wrong finding actively damages
the change. You also lose the distinction between “must fix before this
ships” and “worth knowing about,” which means the next change carries
all fifteen again.

This chapter builds one operation in TypeScript, field by field: you send
some text to a server, and text comes back. An agentic workflow rests
on that operation. Every diagram, review, judge and guard rule in the
twelve chapters after this one is that single operation wrapped in struc-

A large language model — LLM for short — is a very large mathe-

distribution over what text comes next. It was fitted to that job by be-

numbers, called weights, that do not change while you use them.

2 Introduction
The picture above is an agent : a program that calls a model in a loop,
runs whatever tool the model asks for, and stops when the model stops
asking. It is what you are going to build.
A workflow is a fixed sequence of jobs that a piece of work passes
through, where each job has one responsibility and a defined output.
An agentic workflow is one in which some of those jobs are carried out
by a language model rather than by a person or by code you wrote in
advance.
What travels along those arrows is one JSON object — which model to
ask, the standing instruction, the tools it may call, and every instruction
and reply so far, because the model keeps nothing between calls. Chapter
1 builds the first few of those fields and Chapter 2 the rest, and Chapter
2 shows the whole object once you have written enough of it to read it.

Introduction 3
erything sent and received so far, and one response. The model retains
nothing between calls: everything it knows on call n is what you put
in call n , which makes carrying state forward your program’s job rather
than the model’s. (Chapter 1)
Tools. Descriptions of capabilities — read a file, run a query against a
database, call a service somewhere else — listed in the request’s tools
field. The model cannot execute any of them itself; it can only reply
that it wants to, naming a tool and its arguments, and your code decides
whether to run it and sends the result back. Every constraint on what
an agent can do lives on your side of that line. (Chapter 2)
A loop. Call the model, execute whatever tool it asked for, append the
result, call again, until it stops asking. The loop needs a way to stop,
because a model that keeps requesting tools will keep being handed them.

A token budget is a soft limit you impose: the number of tokens you
have decided a piece of work is allowed to consume in total, across every
request it makes. Nothing enforces it but you, and it exists because the
context window is generous enough that a runaway loop can burn a great
deal of money without ever tripping the hard limit.
The context window protects the model and the token budget protects
you, and only the first of them is switched on by default.

different results, so a run that came out right once does not tell

real, and being confidently wrong is expensive. That case takes two
things. A model has to be able to act, and whatever establishes that the
work is right has to be something other than the run that produced it.

An agent is a program in a loop with a language model.
The program sends a request with a list of tools the model
may ask for, each described in plain words: what it does,

next request, and sends it again, until the model asks for

piece of work passes through from start to finish, where
each job is either an agent or ordinary code. The jobs
run serially, and where several run in parallel, the next

None of that touches whether the work is any good.
Everything in this chapter is about capacity: how much can go in, how
much comes back, what it costs. The agent from Chapter 3, running
comfortably inside its budget with a healthy cache hit rate, can still
produce a fix that does not fix anything, describe a test it never ran,
and finish with end_turn and an articulate summary of work it did not
do.

2 Introduction
The picture above is an agent : a program that calls a model in a loop,
runs whatever tool the model asks for, and stops when the model stops
asking. It is what you are going to build.
A workflow is a fixed sequence of jobs that a piece of work passes
through, where each job has one responsibility and a defined output.
An agentic workflow is one in which some of those jobs are carried out
by a language model rather than by a person or by code you wrote in
advance.
What travels along those arrows is one JSON object — which model to
ask, the standing instruction, the tools it may call, and every instruction
and reply so far, because the model keeps nothing between calls. Chapter
1 builds the first few of those fields and Chapter 2 the rest, and Chapter
2 shows the whole object once you have written enough of it to read it.

Conclusion 197
Take them in this order, because it is the order of benefit per unit of
disruption:
1. Write the plan first, by hand, for one change. No tooling. A
markdown file with intent, four falsifiable acceptance criteria, and three
non-goals, which costs twenty minutes. Afterwards, “is it done?” is an-
swered by running four commands rather than by forming an impression.
2. Prove one test can fail. Pick the test you most rely on, break the
code it guards, and watch what the suite does. Roughly one time in five,
in the author’s experience, the test does not go red.
3. Add one guard rule , for whichever rule your team breaks most
often. Ten lines and an exit code, run wherever your other checks run,
make it a program rather than a policy document.
4. Then review, and only then.

Multi-lens review is the most

to read. It pays for itself against a written plan, and it produces noise
against a vague one — so it comes after step 1 has become a habit, not
before.

Four things it does not mean, each of which you can check against the

exists anywhere in the system, which is exactly why Chapter 6 has you
